American Civil Liberties. The fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals protected by the US Constitution and Bill of Rights, including free speech, religious practice, due process, and protection from unreasonable searches. Throughout American history, these liberties have been contested, restricted in crises, and gradually expanded through court decisions and constitutional amendments.

The Bill of Rights—the first ten amendments, ratified in seventeen ninety-one—established the core civil liberties: free speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition. The Fourteenth Amendment in eighteen sixty-eight extended rights protections against state governments, not just the federal government, through the incorporation doctrine.

Civil liberties have repeatedly contracted in crises. The Alien and Sedition Acts in seventeen ninety-eight, internment during World War II, and McCarthyism in the nineteen fifties all saw suspension of speech and due process. The American Civil Liberties Union, founded in nineteen twenty, became the primary defender of civil liberties through litigation and advocacy. The Warren Court from nineteen fifty-three to nineteen sixty-nine dramatically expanded civil liberties protections through landmark decisions like Miranda v. Arizona, Gideon v. Wainwright, and desegregation decisions.

Watergate from nineteen seventy-three to nineteen seventy-four was catalyzed partly by civil liberties concerns about executive overreach and unconstitutional government surveillance. The ongoing tension between security and freedom, between majority will and individual rights, defines much of American constitutional law and politics. Modern debates pit civil liberties like speech and privacy against security concerns in contexts of terrorism, immigration, and digital surveillance.
